beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Sai Pranavi J. This video is about a keyword scorer that was crying wolf, marking routine filings as Critical because of one word in the title, and a second-opinion pass, running locally, that catches it.
beats.new_visual_element: Personal-intro card: fellow's name + one-line summary of what the video covers, spoken

shot.note: Same pattern as this fellow's other episodes' B01.

beats.narration_text: Two real items landed in this pipeline's Critical bucket last month. One was a routine Medicare payment rule. The other was a boilerplate filing about cabinet wiring at Nasdaq. Neither one was actually urgent.
beats.new_visual_element: Two title cards side by side, each stamped '10/CRITICAL' and '9/CRITICAL'

beats.narration_text: Here's why. The scorer reads the full text and adds three points the moment it sees the word 'immediate' or 'emergency', anywhere in the title, no matter what it's actually attached to.
beats.new_visual_element: The real scoring rule, quoted verbatim: if (text.includes('immediate') || text.includes('emergency')) score += 3;

shot.note: [Source: C2-VERIFICATION.md 'The problem', quoting calculateBasicUrgency()] Code quoted verbatim, not paraphrased.

beats.narration_text: Look at where that word actually shows up. The Medicare rule's 'emergency' comes from 'Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act', a law's full legal name. The Nasdaq filing's 'immediate' comes from 'Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness', standard boilerplate every routine rule change uses. The scorer can't see the difference between a real emergency and a law's title.
beats.new_visual_element: Both real titles, the trigger word highlighted in place, with a caption showing what it's actually part of

shot.note: [Source: C2-VERIFICATION.md 'The problem'; real titles from live DB rows id 4 and id 966/967]

beats.narration_text: The fix doesn't touch the original scorer at all. Every item that would trigger an alert gets a second look, a small model running locally on this machine reads the title and asks: is this actually urgent, or is that just an incidental word? If it says the alert would be noise, that one item gets held back. If the model itself fails for any reason, nothing breaks, the item just goes through exactly as it would have before this check ever existed.
beats.new_visual_element: Flow diagram: item -> local model review -> confirm (goes through) or downgrade (held back); a third branch labeled 'model fails -> goes through anyway (fail-open)'

shot.note: [Source: C2-VERIFICATION.md 'The design'] The fail-open branch must be shown explicitly, not just the happy path.

beats.narration_text: I tested it against exactly those two cases, plus a real enforcement case, an actual SEC insider-trading charge, to make sure it doesn't just downgrade everything. Both routine filings: flagged as noise. The real enforcement case: left alone, exactly as it should be.
beats.new_visual_element: A 3-row results table: Medicare (downgrade), Nasdaq (downgrade), SEC insider-trading case (untouched, small label 'not reviewed — below alert threshold')

shot.note: [Source: C2-VERIFICATION.md 'Live verification' table. Label per FACTCHECK.md item #1: the SEC case was never sent to the model, not reviewed-and-approved.] All 3 rows visible together.

beats.narration_text: Three things this doesn't claim. The correction is cautious, it moves these off Critical, not all the way down to where a person might put them. It's tested against two known patterns, not a full benchmark. And it adds real time, reviewing everything above the alert line could add several minutes to a single run.
beats.new_visual_element: 3 limitation cards, stated plainly, not minimized

shot.note: [Source: C2-VERIFICATION.md 'What's honest and NOT overclaimed here'] Kept at full weight per FACTCHECK.md resolution — no softening.
